title: 100+ Vendors, 100 Different Invoice Formats: How F&B Companies Tame Supplier Chaos with AI
summary: F&B companies with 100+ vendors face invoice extraction chaos—each supplier uses different formats. Learn how Peakflo's AI OCR handles diverse vendor formats and auto-matches to POs.
body_text: **TL;DR:** F&B companies with 100+ vendors lose 60 to 100 staff-hours per month to manual invoice processing because every supplier uses a different format, naming convention, and field structure—making traditional OCR unreliable. Peakflo's adaptive AI learns each vendor's unique invoice format, fuzzy-matches supplier item names to PO descriptions, and handles missing fields gracefully, reducing manual intervention by up to 80% and processing invoices in minutes rather than days. Why Does F&B Vendor Invoice Processing Break Down at Scale? F&B accounts payable teams face a problem that most industries do not: their supplier base is genuinely diverse in ways that go far beyond format differences. A snack brand, a restaurant group, or a food distributor may work simultaneously with a fresh produce farm that hand-writes delivery notes, a packaging supplier that emails Excel files, a cold-chain logistics company with a custom ERP, and dozens of other vendors—each with their own invoicing logic, item naming conventions, and payment term formats. The result is an invoice pile that looks different every single day. Some invoices carry no invoice number at all. Some use internal product codes that bear no resemblance to the buyer’s PO line items. Some arrive with partial quantities because the vendor shipped what was available and will invoice the remainder later. For AI invoice processing for F&B distributors to work in this environment, it must do something traditional OCR cannot: adapt to each vendor rather than requiring each vendor to adapt to a template. This guide explains why F&B vendor invoice format inconsistency is a systemic problem, what it costs in real staff-hours, and how modern AI-powered extraction solves it—including the specific techniques that make fuzzy matching and missing-field handling work in practice. Why F&B Companies Face This Challenge More Than Other Industries Most industries work with a relatively contained supplier base. A manufacturer sources from a handful of raw material suppliers, many of whom use standardized EDI formats. A professional services firm receives invoices from a small pool of contractors. But F&B operations are structurally different in three ways that compound the invoice format problem. Highly fragmented supplier ecosystem. An F&B company’s vendor base typically spans multiple tiers: primary ingredient suppliers, secondary ingredient suppliers, packaging vendors, cold storage providers, contract manufacturers, maintenance contractors, and logistics partners. Each tier has its own accounting norms and tools. A small produce farm uses a basic invoice template from a free accounting app. A multinational ingredient supplier sends structured PDFs generated by SAP. Both land in the same AP inbox and need to be processed with equal efficiency. Daily ordering and high invoice volume. Unlike quarterly or monthly procurement cycles common in other industries, F&B operations often order fresh ingredients daily or several times per week. This means invoice volume is inherently high relative to company size. A restaurant group running 10 outlets may receive 200+ invoices per week across all suppliers—far more than a similarly-sized business in a different sector. Minimal supplier standardization leverage. F&B buyers, especially in Southeast Asia, typically lack the purchasing power to mandate invoice format compliance from small local suppliers. Asking a wet market produce supplier to restructure their billing to match a buyer’s ERP requirements is unrealistic. The AP team must accept invoices as they come and build the intelligence to handle them. According to research published by Ardent Partners , the average cost to process a single invoice manually is between $10 and $15 USD, with exception-heavy industries like F&B trending toward the higher end. Multiply that across hundreds of monthly invoices and the cost compounds quickly. What Does Vendor Invoice Format Chaos Actually Cost? The real cost is not just monetary—it is measured in staff-hours and delayed payments. Finance teams at F&B companies with large supplier bases report spending 3 to 5 hours per vendor per month on invoice-related tasks: manually keying data, investigating mismatched line items, chasing vendors for missing details, and reconciling discrepancies between received quantities and invoiced amounts. At 20 active vendors, that is 60 to 100 staff-hours lost every month to a single process that generates no strategic value. At 100+ vendors, the math becomes untenable without additional headcount. Yet hiring more AP staff does not solve the underlying problem—it scales the manual process rather than replacing it. There are also downstream consequences. Payment delays from processing backlogs damage supplier relationships, particularly with smaller vendors who depend on timely cash flow. Duplicate payments—common when the same invoice arrives in two formats or under two slightly different vendor names—are hard to catch manually. And audit trails become fragmented when invoice data lives partly in the ERP, partly in email, and partly in spreadsheets maintained by individual AP staff members. The prevent duplicate invoices and payments challenge alone is significant: without a system that identifies an invoice by multiple data points rather than just its number, duplicate submissions from vendors with inconsistent numbering conventions slip through undetected. Why Traditional OCR Cannot Solve the Multi-Format Problem Traditional OCR—optical character recognition—converts invoice images into machine-readable text. The problem is that OCR alone does not understand what the text means or where specific data fields should be. To extract the invoice number, amount, vendor name, and line items reliably, rule-based OCR systems depend on templates: predefined layouts that specify where each field appears on the page. This works reasonably well when a company processes invoices from a small, stable set of suppliers with consistent document formats. It fails immediately when applied to a diverse vendor base, for several reasons. First, template-based systems require a new template to be created and validated for each vendor. At 100+ vendors, this is an upfront investment of hundreds of hours, and templates need updating every time a vendor changes their invoice layout. Second, even within a single vendor’s invoices, variation occurs—different staff members may produce the document, the software may be updated, or seasonal invoices may include additional fields. Third, template-based systems have no way to handle missing fields. If an invoice number is absent, the system returns an extraction error rather than inferring what it can from the available data. The deeper problem is item description matching. Traditional OCR can extract the text “chocolate flavored S premix” from an invoice, but it cannot know that this matches the PO line item “ice cream powder chocolate soft serve premix.” That requires semantic understanding—the ability to assess similarity rather than equality. How AI Learns Each Vendor’s Invoice Format Modern AI-powered extraction, unlike template-based OCR, does not require predefined layouts. Instead, it uses machine learning models trained on millions of invoice documents to understand the structure of invoices in general, and then adapts to specific vendors through exposure to their actual documents. When Peakflo’s AI-powered invoice capture processes a vendor’s invoice for the first time, it extracts as many fields as possible using general invoice intelligence. Fields it cannot extract with high confidence are flagged for human review. When a reviewer corrects the extraction—confirming that a particular text block is the invoice number, or that a specific line is a freight charge rather than a product—that correction trains the system’s vendor-specific model. After 5 to 10 invoices from a given vendor, the AI begins recognizing that vendor’s specific layout and field patterns reliably. After 20 to 30 invoices, it handles that vendor with minimal exceptions. This learning compounds over time: the longer Peakflo is used with a given supplier, the better it performs, and the fewer exceptions reach human reviewers. Critically, this learning is additive. Adding a new vendor does not degrade performance on existing vendors. The system maintains separate recognition profiles for each supplier, so growing the vendor base does not increase the error rate on well-established suppliers. Fuzzy Matching: How AI Resolves Mismatched Item Names Even after successful invoice extraction, F&B AP teams face a second matching problem: supplier item names rarely match the buyer’s PO descriptions exactly. This is not a mistake—it is a natural consequence of two organizations maintaining separate product catalogs independently. Peakflo’s auto PO matching uses fuzzy matching algorithms that assess similarity rather than requiring exact text equality. When comparing a supplier’s line item against open PO lines, the system evaluates multiple signals simultaneously. Textual similarity: how many words or character sequences overlap between the supplier description and the PO description Semantic meaning: whether the two descriptions refer to the same type of product based on the AI’s understanding of food and beverage item categories Numerical alignment: whether the unit price, quantity, and unit of measure are consistent across the invoice and PO Historical match patterns: whether this vendor has previously matched this specific item description to this PO line By combining these signals, the AI can confidently match “chocolate flavored S premix” to “ice cream powder chocolate soft serve premix”—two descriptions that share only one exact word but clearly refer to the same product in context. Items that cannot be matched with sufficient confidence are flagged as exceptions and routed to an AP reviewer with a suggested match displayed alongside for quick approval. To understand how this integrates with the broader three-way matching process, the AI agents three-way matching guide provides a detailed walkthrough of how purchase order reconciliation works end-to-end. How Missing Invoice Fields Are Handled One of the most disruptive scenarios in F&B vendor invoice processing is the invoice that arrives without standard fields. No invoice number. No line-item descriptions—just a total amount. Or an invoice from a vendor whose name in the system differs slightly from how they sign their documents. Peakflo handles missing and ambiguous fields through a combination of inference and graceful exception handling. When an invoice number is absent, the system attempts to construct a unique identifier using available fields: vendor name, date, and total amount. This synthetic identifier enables the invoice to be tracked and deduplicated within the system without blocking the extraction process. When a vendor name on an invoice does not exactly match the vendor record in the ERP, the system uses fuzzy vendor matching—similar to item matching—to identify the most likely candidate from the vendor master. If confidence is high, it auto-maps the invoice to that vendor. If confidence is below threshold, it presents the suggested match to an AP reviewer. For partial deliveries—a common occurrence in fresh produce and perishable goods procurement—the system compares invoiced quantities against goods receipt notes entered by warehouse staff. When the received quantity differs from the invoiced quantity, the discrepancy is flagged at the line-item level, not the invoice level, so the portions that match can proceed toward payment while the exception is resolved in isolation. This approach is described in more detail in the three-way matching accounts payable guide. How Peakflo’s AI Handles 100+ Vendor Invoice Formats Peakflo’s accounts payable automation platform is built specifically to handle the kind of supplier diversity that F&B companies face. The key capabilities that address multi-vendor format chaos are: Adaptive OCR with vendor-specific learning. The extraction engine learns each vendor’s document layout over time, continuously improving accuracy without requiring manual template configuration. New vendors are onboarded automatically as their invoices arrive. Fuzzy PO matching with semantic understanding. The matching algorithm handles synonym-level differences between supplier item descriptions and PO line items, reducing the manual reconciliation workload that normally accompanies diverse supplier bases. Missing field inference. When standard fields like invoice numbers are absent, the AI extracts available data and constructs logical identifiers to keep processing moving. Reviewers see exactly which fields were inferred and can correct them in context. Vendor-specific tolerance rules. AP managers can configure matching thresholds per vendor category—allowing, for example, a 3% price variance for spot-market produce vendors while enforcing exact matching for contracted suppliers. Continuous improvement loop. Every exception that a reviewer resolves is fed back into the vendor’s recognition model, so accuracy improves over time without IT intervention or manual retraining. Vendor portal for digital submission. Peakflo’s vendor portal gives suppliers a self-service channel to submit invoices digitally, reducing email-based friction and enabling real-time submission status tracking—without requiring vendors to change how they format their invoices. Vendor data quality underlies everything: maintaining accurate vendor master records is a prerequisite for reliable auto-matching. The vendor data repository management guide and automated vendor validation checks guide cover how to keep vendor records clean as the supplier base grows. Traditional OCR vs. AI-Powered Extraction: A Direct Comparison The difference between rule-based OCR and modern AI extraction becomes clear when mapped against the specific challenges of F&B vendor invoice processing. The typical deployment follows six steps. Step 1: Audit your current vendor invoice mix. Catalog all active vendors and document the formats they currently use. Identify where manual intervention is highest—these are the vendors and exception types that will show the earliest improvement after AI deployment. Step 2: Connect your invoice intake channels. Configure the system to receive invoices from all existing channels: shared AP email inboxes, vendor portal uploads, and ERP integrations. No changes are required on the vendor side. Step 3: Process historical invoices to build vendor profiles. Run the last 3 to 6 months of invoices through the AI engine. This batch-trains vendor recognition models and builds the fuzzy match dictionary for your specific PO item names and supplier descriptions. Step 4: Configure PO matching rules by vendor category. Set quantity and price variance tolerances appropriate for each supplier type. Fresh produce vendors typically warrant looser tolerances than contracted dry goods suppliers. Step 5: Define exception routing workflows. Set up exception queues and assign approvers by exception type, invoice value, or vendor category. Exceptions should reach the right reviewer immediately rather than sitting in a shared inbox. Step 6: Monitor and refine over 60 to 90 days. Review AI confidence scores weekly. Reviewer corrections feed automatically into vendor models. Most teams reach 95%+ straight-through processing rates within the first quarter. Results F&B Finance Teams Can Expect The measurable outcomes of AI-powered F&B vendor invoice processing fall into three categories: time savings, accuracy improvements, and cost reduction. Research from Gartner indicates that organizations using AI-powered AP automation reduce invoice processing exceptions by up to 60%, which directly translates to reduced staff burden and faster payment cycles. A report by Deloitte on digital finance transformation notes that finance teams that automate transactional processes like invoice matching redirect an average of 30% of staff capacity toward analytics and business partnering activities—a significant shift for F&B finance directors seeking to add strategic value. Industry data from APQC’s Finance and Accounting benchmarks shows that best-in-class AP organizations process invoices at a cost 5x lower than bottom-quartile performers, with automation being the primary differentiator. For additional context on industry-specific automation trends in food and beverage supply chains, the Hackett Group’s AP performance benchmarks provide useful comparative data across sectors. Our Verdict: Is AI Invoice Processing Right for Your F&B Operation? After analyzing the F&B accounts payable landscape, here is our assessment of when AI invoice processing delivers the strongest return. Strongly recommended if: Your operation has 30 or more active vendors with different invoice formats Your AP team spends more than 20 hours per week on manual data entry and exception resolution You experience regular payment delays due to invoice processing backlogs You have recurring issues with duplicate payments, mismatched line items, or partial delivery reconciliation Your vendor base includes small local suppliers who will not or cannot standardize their invoicing Consider a phased approach if: Your vendor base is below 15 suppliers, most of whom send structured digital invoices You are still in the process of digitizing receiving workflows (AI matching requires goods receipt data to function) Your ERP does not yet have PO data structured for automated matching Not the right moment if: Your AP volume is fewer than 50 invoices per month across all vendors—the ROI case is harder to justify at that scale You have no digital PO process in place, as three-way matching requires purchase order data as a reference point Our Recommendation: For most F&B companies operating in Southeast Asia with 30+ vendors and daily or weekly ordering cycles, the ROI case for AI invoice processing is clear. The break-even point—where automation savings offset implementation costs—typically occurs within 3 to 6 months. The longer the delay, the more staff-hours accumulate on a problem that scales linearly with vendor count. Frequently Asked Questions Why do F&B companies struggle more with vendor invoice formats than other industries? F&B companies typically source from a highly fragmented supplier base—fresh produce farms, dry goods wholesalers, packaging suppliers, cold-chain logistics partners, and more. Unlike manufacturing, where suppliers are fewer and more standardized, F&B operations can involve 100+ active vendors, many of which are small local suppliers who create invoices manually or with basic accounting tools. Each vendor independently decides how to number invoices, label items, and structure payment terms, creating enormous format diversity that overwhelms rule-based OCR systems. What happens when a vendor doesn’t include an invoice number? When a vendor omits an invoice number—which is common among smaller F&B suppliers—traditional OCR systems either fail the extraction or flag the document for manual review. Peakflo’s AI handles this gracefully by using other available data points such as vendor name, invoice date, line item totals, and PO reference numbers to uniquely identify and record the invoice. This prevents bottlenecks and keeps the AP queue moving even when field data is incomplete. How does AI match invoice line items when supplier item names don’t match PO descriptions? AI-powered fuzzy matching looks beyond exact text to understand semantic similarity. For example, if a PO lists “ice cream powder chocolate soft serve premix” but the supplier invoice says “chocolate flavored S premix,” the system analyzes multiple signals—partial word matches, item category context, pricing alignment, unit of measure, and historical matching patterns—to confidently link the two. Over time, the AI learns each vendor’s specific naming conventions and improves match accuracy automatically. How long does it take for AI OCR to learn a new vendor’s invoice format? Most AI systems begin recognizing vendor-specific patterns after processing 5 to 10 invoices from that supplier. Full learning—where the system handles the vendor’s format with minimal exceptions—typically occurs within the first 20 to 30 invoices. Once learned, the vendor profile is retained permanently, so even infrequent suppliers are handled efficiently when they resurface. What is the cost of manual invoice processing for F&B companies with 100+ vendors? Finance teams report spending 3 to 5 hours per vendor per month on invoice-related tasks including data entry, exception resolution, and PO matching. For a company with 20 or more active vendors, that equals 60 to 100 staff-hours lost monthly to this single task. At fully loaded labor costs, this typically translates to significant annual expenditure—all on work that generates no strategic value and can be automated. Can AI handle partial deliveries where the invoice amount differs from the PO? Yes. Peakflo’s AI is built to handle partial deliveries by comparing the received quantity (confirmed by warehouse or receiving staff) against both the original PO quantity and the invoiced quantity. When discrepancies are detected, the system flags the specific line items with the variance amount and routes the exception for approval rather than halting the entire invoice. This keeps payment for fulfilled portions on schedule while exceptions are resolved. Does Peakflo require vendors to change how they send invoices? No. Peakflo is designed to accept invoices exactly as vendors send them—PDF, scanned images, Excel, email attachments, or via the vendor portal. Vendors do not need to change their invoicing format or adopt new systems. The AI adapts to each vendor’s existing format, which means adoption is frictionless and supplier relationships are not disrupted. What accuracy rate can F&B companies expect from AI invoice extraction? AI-powered invoice extraction typically achieves 92 to 96% accuracy on initial deployment, improving to 97 to 99% after the system has processed several hundred invoices and learned vendor-specific patterns. Accuracy also depends on invoice image quality—clearly scanned or digital PDFs consistently outperform handwritten or low-resolution documents. How does Peakflo handle invoices received in different languages or currencies? Peakflo supports multi-language invoice processing and multi-currency handling, which is particularly relevant for F&B companies in Southeast Asia sourcing from suppliers across Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and beyond. The system can extract and normalize fields from invoices written in English, Bahasa Indonesia, Thai, and other regional languages, and automatically converts currencies based on configured exchange rates. What is three-way matching and why is it important for F&B AP teams? Three-way matching is the process of verifying that a supplier invoice, the corresponding purchase order, and the goods receipt note (GRN) all agree before a payment is approved. For F&B companies, this is critical because perishable goods deliveries often involve quantity variances, substitutions, or partial shipments. Automated three-way matching catches discrepancies before payment, reducing overpayments, duplicate payments, and fraud exposure. How does Peakflo’s vendor portal help standardize invoice submission? Peakflo’s vendor portal gives suppliers a self-service channel to submit invoices, check payment status, and update their details—without requiring email chains or phone follow-ups. While the portal encourages digital submission, it does not force format compliance. Vendors who prefer to email PDFs or upload scanned documents can still do so, and the AI extraction engine handles all formats equally. F&B vendor invoice format inconsistency is not a problem that scales away—it compounds as vendor bases grow and ordering frequency increases. Traditional OCR and manual processing cannot keep pace with 100+ suppliers sending invoices in fundamentally different formats. AI-powered extraction with adaptive vendor learning, fuzzy PO matching, and graceful missing-field handling is the only scalable answer. Peakflo’s AP automation platform is purpose-built for the diversity of the F&B supply chain. If your team is spending dozens of hours each month reconciling invoices that should be processed automatically, the time to act is now. title: HR Pulse: Navigating Today’s Job Market
body_text: Current Job Market Landscape Broadening digital access is projected to be the most transformative trend, not only among technology-related developments but across all major trends. In fact, 60% of employers expect it to reshape their business by 2030. These shifts are expected to have a dual impact on the job market, simultaneously driving the fastest-growing and fastest-declining roles. As a result, demand is surging for technology-related skills, particularly in AI and Big Data, Networks, and Cybersecurity. Furthermore, technological literacy is anticipated to be the top fastest-growing skill area. [Source [i]] The Growing Role of AI in Recruitment AI's role in recruitment is growing, making it essential for job seekers to understand how to use these tools effectively. Michael Garcia , Talent Acquisition Team Lead at CAE USA , emphasizes the importance of staying ahead of AI trends. He advises job seekers to anticipate new roles that have never existed before and to use AI for interview preparation. Michael explains that as AI increasingly shapes the recruitment process, knowing how to leverage AI tools can give job seekers a competitive edge. For instance, proficiency in data analytics can help candidates stand out in a market where AI relies on data-driven decisions, making them valuable to any organization. Additionally, using AI for interview preparation can provide candidates with tailored insights and realistic practice, boosting their confidence. However, it's not just about the tools; the real differentiator is the ability to combine technical expertise with genuine authenticity. By embracing current trends, today’s job seekers can position themselves for both present-day opportunities and future roles that AI will help create. In-Demand Skills in the Market As industries evolve, certain skill sets are becoming increasingly valuable. Professionals looking to build or pivot their careers can consider focusing on high-growth fields, including: [Source [ii]] Machine Learning & AI: The rise of artificial intelligence is creating demand for specialists in automation, predictive analytics, and AI-driven decision-making. Cybersecurity: With the increasing number of cyber threats, both technical and functional cybersecurity professionals are in high demand. Data Privacy: As data regulations tighten worldwide, companies need experts to ensure compliance and protect user information. Healthcare & Biotech: Advancements in technology are driving opportunities in health sciences, from telemedicine to medical device development. Engineering & Technology: Technical roles remain vital across industries, including aerospace, software development, and electrical engineering. Freelance & Nontraditional Roles: The gig economy is expanding, providing opportunities for independent professionals in various disciplines. By focusing on these high-growth areas, professionals can enhance their career prospects and stay ahead in the competitive job market. Job Search Strategies for Success Linda Quezada , Talent Acquisition Specialist at CAE USA shares key strategies to help job seekers navigate the job market with confidence and clarity. One of her key takeaways is that planning matters . By taking a strategic approach to a job search, you can significantly increase your chances of success. Tip 1: Define your clear goals Start by understanding the type of career or role you want. Identify your strengths, set specific objectives, and visualize what success looks like for you. Having clear goals allows you to conduct a more focused and time-efficient job search. Tip 2: Optimize your Resume and Digital Presence Ensure your resume is up to date and tailored to the roles you are applying for. Polish your LinkedIn profile and leverage digital platforms to expand your visibility and connect with potential employers. Tip 3: Tailor Your Applications Customize your resume and cover letter for each job application. Highlight the skills and experiences that best match the company’s needs and demonstrate how you can bring value to the roles. Tip 4: Develop Soft Skills Effective communication, teamwork, and leadership abilities are in high demand. Employers are looking for candidates who not only meet the job requirements but also bring adaptability, initiative, and a strong cultural fit to the team. Take away: Implementing effective job search strategies can significantly benefit job seekers. Maximized Efficiency: Focuses applicants efforts on the most promising and career-aligned opportunities. Enhanced Visibility: Helps applicants stand out to employers in a competitive market. Higher Success Rate: Boosts an applicants chances of securing the job you desire. Source: Top Job Search Tips for Landing Your Dream Role Job Boards: Your Path to Recognition Once you have a clear understanding of your goals and the roles you want to pursue, it is time to identify the best job boards to help you stand out. With so many options available, it can be overwhelming. Linda’s recommendation is to focus on quality over quantity to ensure your applications get noticed. Here are some of the top job boards to consider. Indeed One of the most popular and comprehensive job search engines, thanks to the sheer volume of job posting across industries. It is simple interface and keyword/location filters make it easy to find relevant opportunities quickly. LinkedIn LinkedIn’s job board offers a seamless application process. Once your profile is set up, you can apply to many roles with just a few clicks. Plus, the platform allows you to network directly with recruiters and hiring managers, giving you a strategic edge. Dice If you are in the tech industry, Dice is a top choice. It is a job board built specifically for tech roles, offering helpful features like filtering jobs by salary range, skills, or experience level and making it easier to find the right fit. Levels.fyi Originally known for its compensation transparency, Levels.fyi now also includes a job board. Key features include: Monetary Value Estimates: See the estimated total value of compensation packages, including salary, equity, and bonuses. Perk and Benefit Data: Compare benefits across companies to understand what each employer truly offers beyond the paycheck. The Impact of Your Network A robust network can significantly enhance your chances of securing your desired job or finding a mentor to help you achieve that long-awaited promotion. Building a strong network however can be challenging, especially if your current network is limited. Research indicates that Americans without a college education today have experienced a much more dramatic decline in the size of their social circle than have those with four-year degrees. Additionally, when parents have a smaller social circle, it limits the opportunities for first-generation college students to observationally learn about different careers and form professional connections with those who also earned college degrees. Consequently, this can lead to a lack of confidence during the job search process. [Source [iii]] To help navigate your job search and expand your network, here are some valuable tips: Seek Out New Opportunities Actively seek out networking opportunities through industry events, conferences, webinars, social media, and professional organizations. Leverage Existing Connections: Reach out to friends, family, and colleagues to explore potential job leads and mentorship opportunities. Be Intentional : Focus on building strategic, meaningful connections that align with your career goals. Leverage Alumni Networks: Reach out to alumni in your field for advice or referrals. Informational Interviews: Schedule short chats with professionals in your desired role to learn about their career paths. LinkedIn Networking: Send personalized connection requests. Engage with posts from industry leaders or potential employers. Upskill Continuously: - Stay Updated: Follow industry trends and advancements. - Gain Certifications: Pursue advanced certifications to enhance your expertise. - Seek Feedback: Regularly ask for constructive feedback to improve. For inspiration, read about one of CAE’s employees, David Taylor, MS, MBA, PMP® Systems Engineer who advanced his career by intentionally and strategically networking. HR Pulse: Valuable Insights for Early Career Professionals – Lessons Shared from Those Who Have Been There | CAE A further resource is How to Land Your Dream Job in 2025: A Step by Step Guide from LinkedIn. Maintain Professionalism After an Interview Navigating the post-interview phase is crucial for leaving a lasting positive impression and enhancing your chances of securing the job. Here are five essential steps to follow your interview to maintain professionalism and keep your job search on track. 1. Send a Thoughtful Thank You It is always a great idea to follow up with everyone who interviewed you. Sending a personalized thank-you note or email within a day of your interview can make a significant difference. Take a moment to address each person by name, share your appreciation for their time, and mention something specific from your conversation. Feel free to reaffirm your interest in the role, but even if you have decided the position is not the right fit, a thank-you message shows your professionalism, gratitude, and strong personal branding. 2. Follow Up with the Recruiter Following your interview, it is important to touch base with the person who coordinated it, whether that is an internal recruiter, a third-party agency, or an HR manager. This step is not just about being polite; it can also be a strategic move. By reconnecting, you may gain access to valuable feedback that could help you improve your performance or address any concerns that came up during the interview. This proactive approach can enhance your chances of success in future interviews. 3. Follow Up Professionally If the interviewer has provided a timeline for the subsequent steps, it is important to adhere to it. However, should you not receive any communication after a reasonable period, it is entirely appropriate to send a courteous follow-up message. In this message, express your continued interest in the position and politely inquire about the status of the hiring process. title: RUF Enters the Ring with a Heavyweight Boxer
summary: Few venues are more appropriate for wild supercar debuts than the Goodwood Festival of Speed. body_text: Few venues are more appropriate for wild supercar debuts than the Goodwood Festival of Speed. The revelry supporting the annual romp up the hill at Goodwood Estate in West Sussex begins today, and among the big introductions is RUF Automobile’s newest creation, the B8. But the B8 isn’t the German manufacturer’s latest car; it’s an engine. More specifically, the B8, short for Boxer 8, is an all-new, 4.8-liter twin-turbocharged eight-cylinder boxer engine making 1000 horsepower and 738 pound-feet of torque. RUF lead engineer, Marc Brunner (left), with company principal Alois Ruf and the stunning B8 engine. Hans-Dieter Seufert To show off this marvel of engineering, RUF packaged the development motor, known internally as the Erprober (Tester), in one of its CTR3 supercars, which has been lengthened by nearly four inches to accommodate the new powerplant in place of its traditional twin-turbo flat-six. “The B8 is not yet a production model but serves as a dedicated testbed for technologies that will shape a future RUF model,” the company said in a press release. “Each new RUF begins life long before the world sees it, with thousands of kilometers of rigorous testing to ensure its extreme performance is matched with equal parts durability and drivability.” Hans-Dieter Seufert Hans-Dieter Seufert Hans-Dieter Seufert At Goodwood, the B8-powered CTR3 will take part in the Supercar Run twice per day, from Friday through Sunday, with American racer Tanner Foust at the wheel. The car will also be parked in the Supercar Paddock throughout the weekend, with the engine on display. The car’s distinctive livery was designed by Aloisa Ruf, daughter of current head Alois, and utilizes the Blossom Yellow made famous on the company’s CTR Yellow Bird . “I wanted the graphics to tell the story of the car before anyone even heard the engine,” she said. “Every line represents movement, and the flowing form of the number eight became a natural symbol, not only for the new boxer eight-cylinder, but for the endless pursuit of improvement and refinement that has always been part of our family’s philosophy.” RUF says that it “prefers to show its engineering prowess rather than tell, and with each run up the hill, [the company] looks forward to letting the world hear the unique sound of its twin-turbo boxer-eight for the first time.” RUF Automobile All boxer engines are flat engines, but not all flat engines are boxers. The difference lies in the way their opposing pistons connect to the crankshaft. In short, flat engines, like the flat-12 of a Ferrari Testarossa, are 180-degree V-8s, with each pair of opposing pistons sharing a crankpin. As one piston moves in, its opposite piston moves out. In boxer engines, the pistons each have their own crankpins and their movements mirror each other. Porsche and Subaru have long championed the boxer engine, both in four- and six-cylinder configurations. Boxer-eights, however, aren’t exactly prevalent in the world of production cars, though they have powered some memorable race machinery, notably from Porsche. In 1962, the company installed its 1.5-liter Type 753 boxer-eight in its first Formula 1 car, the 804. In the hands of Dan Gurney, the 804 gave Porsche its first and only F1 victory, at the 1962 French Grand Prix. The 2.0-liter Type 771 powered a few 904s, as well as the 906, 910, and 907 sports racers. Perhaps most famous was the 908 sports prototype that debuted at Le Mans in 1968. It utilized a 3.0-liter boxer-eight making around 350 hp. Two of those engines also found their way into 914 street cars, which… whoa. As automotive engineers continue to refine more established engine configurations (the inline-fours and sixes, as well as the V-6s, V-8s, and V-12s of the world), not to mention the whirring electric motors of our inevitable future, this news from RUF is indeed a breath of fresh air. “There are moments in a company’s history that define the future,” said Alois Ruf. “For RUF, the Boxer 8 is one of those moments. A boxer-eight has never been part of our story, or anyone else’s in this form, so we decided to write a new chapter in automotive history. We look forward to letting the engine speak for itself at Goodwood.” The Goodwood Festival of Speed runs through July 12, and much of the event will be livestreamed here . title: Pure Cycle Announces Financial Results For the Three and Nine Months Ended May 31, 2026 and Announces a Board of Directors Transition
body_text: Pure Cycle Announces Financial Results For the Three and Nine Months Ended May 31, 2026 and Announces a Board of Directors Transition Download as PDF July 08, 2026 4:00pm EDT Related Documents Q3 2026 Quarter Ended May 31, 2026 Video Earnings Webcast 10-Q Filing PDF HTML XBRL ZIP HTML Transcript PDF DENVER, July 08, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Pure Cycle Corporation (NASDAQ Capital Market: PCYO) (“Pure Cycle”, the “Company”, “we”, “us” or “our”) announced its financial results for the three and nine months ended May 31, 2026. Pure Cycle reported $2.9 million and $8.6 million of net income for the three and nine months ended May 31, 2026, respectively, which is a 31% and 23% increase in net income from the same periods in 2025 and marks the twenty-eighth consecutive fiscal quarter with positive net income. Pure Cycle reported $0.12 and $0.36 of earnings per fully diluted common share, which is up from $0.09 and $0.29 in the same periods in 2025, a 33% and 24% increase, respectively. Total revenue for the three and nine months ended May 31, 2026 grew 60% and 51%, respectively, over the prior-year periods, driven by growth across both our land development and water segments. Lot sales revenue increased 19% for the quarter and 78% year to date on accelerated development activity at Sky Ranch, while water and wastewater segment revenue increased 119% and 34%, respectively, on higher oil and gas water demand. Our diversified water and land platform was on full display this quarter, as steady, annual-cadence lot deliveries to our national homebuilder partners were complemented by a sharp increase in water sales to oil and gas operators. Monetizing demand across multiple end markets allows us to grow earnings while navigating cyclical trends in the housing industry. For the nine months ended May 31, 2026, our cash balance reflected the accelerated pace of land development at Sky Ranch, where an unseasonably mild winter allowed us to advance our construction schedule. Phase 2D is now approximately 84% complete, Phase 2C is approximately 95% complete, and we expect to substantially complete Phase 2D by the end of fiscal 2026 and collect the related contractual milestone and finished-lot payments with minimal remaining development costs. We have also begun construction activities in Phase 2E, where we expect to complete approximately 159 lots in fiscal 2027, paced to match builder absorption. We typically sign a builder contract before advancing development and recognize revenue under the percentage-of-completion method; with Phase 2E, while we have several builders who have expressed interest, we have chosen to continue development ahead of a signed commitment to take advantage of our seasonal construction windows to be able to complete finished lots for delivery in fiscal 2027. While this departs from our usual process, it reflects our conviction to invest in our business segments developing high demand entry level lots at Sky Ranch and allows us to pace lot construction to Colorado's seasonal construction window. Our cash balance during the period was also impacted by continued investment in new water and wastewater infrastructure within the Sky Ranch community and in our single-family rental business. We hold contracts to construct 23 of the 33 additional rental units planned in Phases 2C and 2D, the majority of which we expect to be available for rent in calendar 2026, and as units are completed we will continue to finance them under our SFR Facility Agreement, replenishing the cash advanced during construction. As we have previously disclosed, we have elected to pause further expansion of our single-family rental segment beyond the units currently under contract, both to assess the impact of the administration's comments on potential future regulation and to better evaluate the segment's return on investment and its contribution to shareholder value. We continue to manage our balance sheet to support growth while returning capital to shareholders. Our ongoing development priorities include land development for future phases at Sky Ranch and investments in water and wastewater infrastructure to support future years of tap sales and to meet the capacity requirements of our oil and gas customers. We intend to continue repurchasing shares under our existing program while reserving sufficient liquidity to fund these projects and selective land acquisitions. Board of Directors Transition The Company announced that Daniel R. Kozlowski has notified the Board of his decision to resign as a director of the Company, effective July 7, 2026. As a significant shareholder, Mr. Kozlowski provided valuable insights and direction to the Board throughout his tenure, and his contributions have been greatly appreciated. The Board thanks Mr. Kozlowski for his service and wishes him well in his future endeavors. The Board will conduct a search for Mr. Kozlowski’s successor and believes that a candidate who brings a shareholder perspective will be a valuable member of the Board. title: Ubicloud's Thin CLIent approach to command line interfaces
summary: Traditionally, a command line interface parses the arguments given by the user, determines the API endpoints, and then submits requests to those endpoints. The program then takes the responses from those endpoints and formats them for display to the user. With Ubicloud's approach, the client doesn't parse any arguments. Instead, it just sends all arguments to a single endpoint, which we’ll call the gateway. The gateway endpoint handles requests and responses.
body_text: Ubicloud's Thin CLIent approach to command line interfaces April 2, 2025 · 4 min read Jeremy Evans Principal Software Engineer Ubicloud has supported both a web and API interface since launch. Recently, we decided to also support a command line interface, so that users can interact with Ubicloud directly from their terminal. To implement the command line interface, we took inspiration from old computer terminals. Everything old is new again. The Traditional Approach Traditionally, command line interface programs that interact with web services work like this. The program parses the arguments given by the user, determines the API endpoints, and then submits requests to those endpoints. The program then takes the responses from those endpoints and formats them for display to the user. We’ll be using the following terms in this post: client: the CLI program the user runs. target: The API endpoint that returns the requested information or makes the requested changes. The traditional approach has two main problems. First, every new feature added to the client requires that users update their client in order to use the feature. This gives up the main advantage of web distribution, which is that users can immediately benefit from new features and bug fixes as soon as you put them into production. Second, it is harder to detect bugs in the command line interface, since bugs will generally occur in the client, on the user's machine, and you have to hope the user reports them. Let's see how we mitigate these issues with the Thin CLIent approach. The Thin CLIent Approach With the Thin CLIent approach, the client does no parsing of the arguments given by the user. Instead, it just sends all arguments to a single endpoint, which we’ll call the gateway. The gateway endpoint handles requests and responses in the following way: It parses the arguments provided by the client, determines the appropriate target endpoints to contact, and the request parameters for those endpoints. It then submits internal API requests to the target endpoints. It handles the responses from the target endpoints, and formats them for display to the user. It then provides the formatted plain text response as the response body to the client. The client prints the body of the response directly to the terminal. Using the Thin CLIent approach offers the following advantages: New features can be added to the command line interface without the user needing to update their client. This brings the advantages of web distribution to command line interfaces. The client can be much smaller in terms of code/implementation size than in the traditional approach, as most of the complexity is moved from the client to the gateway endpoint. The overall complexity is about the same, but complexity in the gateway endpoint is easier to manage than client complexity, as it runs in an environment controlled by Ubicloud. Bugs in the command line interface will generally occur on the gateway endpoint and not in the client. Since the gateway endpoint runs in an environment controlled by Ubicloud, it’s easier to identify and fix such bugs. The vast majority of logic is executed on the gateway endpoint and can be implemented in whatever language you prefer. Ubicloud is implemented in Ruby and we would prefer to use Ruby when we have the option to do so. Some commands require contacting multiple target endpoints. The most common example is if you need information from somewhere before making a request to a target endpoint. For example, if we are requesting a restart of a virtual machine given only the machine’s id, we first need to contact a directory node to get the location of the virtual machine to restart. The Thin CLIent approach makes this faster, as internal requests from the gateway endpoint to the target endpoints have no network latency, so you only pay the latency cost for the single request from the client to the gateway endpoint. The Thin CLIent approach has some disadvantages compared to the traditional approach: All commands require contacting the gateway endpoint, so even getting help output takes some time. Commands that require user input will need multiple requests to the gateway endpoint. A simple example is when the gateway endpoint requests confirmation from the user to permanently delete cloud resources. With Thin CLIents, this requires an extra hop between the user and the gateway. We believe the advantages of the Thin CLIent approach heavily outweigh the disadvantages. Securely Handling Program Execution When using a Thin CLIent approach for a client that executes other programs, you have to take additional care in regards to security. For example, if the gateway endpoint is compromised and instructs the client to run rm -rf / , you do not want the client to execute that. To mitigate the damage a rogue gateway endpoint can inflict on a client, you need to limit the programs the client is allowed to execute, and limit the arguments to those programs. Ubicloud's client (named ubi ), can only execute the following programs: ssh : to connect to a virtual machine via ssh sftp : to connect to a virtual machine via sftp scp : to copy a file/directory from the local computer to a virtual machine or from a virtual machine to the local compute via scp psql : to connect to a PostgreSQL database via psql pg_dump : to dump a single PostgreSQL database using pg_dump pg_dumpall : to dump an entire PostgreSQL database cluster using pg_dumpall ubi will refuse to execute a program that is not one of these 6 programs. Additionally, ubi requires that the program name be one of the arguments it was passed (preventing the server from requesting execution of a different program). Additionally, ubi enforces the following restrictions on the arguments: The arguments must include -- to separate arguments from options (except for pg_dumpall , which does not support this). The arguments must include at most one new argument not in the arguments passed to ubi The new argument must come after -- (for non- pg_dumpall ) or must start with -d (for pg_dumpall ) These restrictions are sufficient to allow the 6 commands above to work safely. It's possible we will need to adjust these restrictions if we support additional programs in the future. The goal will remain to limit the flexibility when executing programs to the minimum needed for the client to function. Command Line Program Configuration Using command line options or arguments for configuration of the client is not possible with the Thin CLIent approach, since the client does not parse them, it only sends them to the gateway endpoint. So you cannot use an approach similar to ubi --gateway https://api.example.com/cli … to specify a custom endpoint. For ubi , we decided to have all program configuration be through environment variables. It would be possible to have the client look for configuration in a file at a known location, but the only required configuration option is the token used for the request (which should be secret), and security-conscious organizations are probably not going to want to store secrets in files on local machines. There are many different systems that handle secret storage, and it's infeasible for ubi to attempt to integrate with all of them. So instead, ubi only deals with environment variables, and users can use whatever secret storage approach they want, as long as they call ubi with the appropriate environment variables set. Command Line Program Development As Ubicloud is written mostly in Ruby, it should come as no surprise that ubi was prototyped in Ruby. However, we do not want to require that our users have Ruby installed in order to use ubi . From our initial planning stages, our goal was to ship dependency-free native clients for popular operating systems, so that users could run `ubi` without installing anything else. We ultimately decided to port the Ruby version to Go. While not as programmer friendly as Ruby, Go is still relatively easy to work with, our engineering team has experience with it, and importantly, it allows us to easily ship native clients for macOS, Linux, and Windows.
